paper_title: How I Aligned Your Model: Scaling Up Multilingual Safety Training with Templates

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Safety alignment for Large Language Models is heavily focused on English with limited multilingual representation, particularly damaging low-resource language performance. Related open training datasets are often limited in size or do not follow region-localized harmful topics to broaden the scope of alignment beyond cultures. We propose a scalable template-based augmentation pipeline to produce massive multilingual refusal and benign corpora, extracting safe templates from harmful prompts, translating them and then filling in the slots with culturally authentic entities, both harmful and benign. As a result, we release MSafeTemp, a validated corpus spanning 60 languages useful for multilingual safety alignment and evaluation. Using the dataset, we show that English-only evaluation misjudges multilingual safety: for several models, attacks that fail in English succeed once translated, while culturally localized variants expose further failures that translation alone misses. We also confirm that augmenting safety training data through templates allows for higher diversity and quality of alignment, resulting in improved safety performance beyond English. MSafeTemp and the respective pipeline are aimed at facilitating research and development of safer and more responsible models for less-represented cultures.

sections.title: ABSTRACT
sections.content: Safety alignment for Large Language Models is heavily focused on English with limited multilingual representation, particularly damaging low-resource language performance. Related open training datasets are often limited in size or do not follow region-localized harmful topics to broaden the scope of alignment beyond cultures. We propose scalable template-based augmentation pipeline to produce massive multilingual refusal and benign corpora, extracting safe templates from harmful prompts, translating them and then filling in the slots with culturally authentic entities, both harmful and benign. As result, we release MSAFETEMP, validated corpus spanning 60 languages useful for multilingual safety alignment and evaluation.1 Using the dataset, we show that English-only evaluation misjudges multilingual safety: for several models, attacks that fail in English succeed once translated, while culturally localized variants expose further failures that translation alone misses. We also confirm that augmenting safety training data through templates allows for higher diversity and quality of alignment, resulting in improved safety performance beyond English. MSAFETEMP and the respective pipeline are aimed at facilitating research and development of safer and more responsible models for less-represented cultures.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: As large language models become more capable, the risks of their misuse grow as well. As result, models undergo extensive safety training and evaluation before deployment. However, existing research consistently shows that red-teaming is much more effective in non-English languages than in English, yet open multilingual safety data remains scarce. Take an English prompt that model reliably refuses, translate it, and adapt it to the specifics of the target culture (a local extremist movement, historical atrocity, community-specific slur): the same model may now comply, even though the harmful intent is unchanged. The curse of safe multilinguality. Existing safety alignment datasets are heavily English-centric, both linguistically and culturally. Collecting data beyond English faces several obstacles: (1) recruiting native speakers for such sensitive tasks is costly and slow, which is challenging at the current pace of global LLM development; (2) human red-teaming is of the highest quality, but rarely covers low-resource languages at scale; (3) machine translation does not produce the locally specific context needed to broaden the scope of the models safety understanding; (4) scalable synthetic data generation or translation with other language models is often blocked by the generators own refusals, since the content is harmful by design. As result, users communicating in low-resource languages are the least protected, and these languages open an easy attack vector for misuse. Multilingual safety can benefit from mix of cross-lingual transfer, stronger general model capabilities, and strong English-focused alignment. However, these effects diminish in extremely low-resource settings, and even more so for culture-specific harms, which depend not on knowledge transfer but on knowledge breadth. Therefore, safety should be treated less as general model capability axis and more as combination of model, language, and culture axes: request reliably 1Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/swiss-ai/MSafeTemp; Code: https:// github.com/swiss-ai/msafetemp. Measuring and closing this gap requires safety data that is multilingual and culturally authentic, not merely translated. Figure 1: The MSAFETEMP pipeline. Original prompt goes through extraction of harmful terms, validation, translation, and targeted judge pass of template. Three branches then produce generic harmful variants (TR), exact-fill benign controls (OR), and culturally localized variants (PH). English (EN) follows the same path without translation. This work. We produce such data at scale in fully automated way by relying on language models instead of human red-teaming experts. We abstract real harmful prompt into template with typed slots and translate the template natively, then refill those slots along two axes. Generic fillers carry the harmful frame into every language at full coverage; second, deliberately selective pass instead admits real local referents from per-language cultural card. Filling the same slots with safe referents gives benign minimal pairs, which serve both to measure over-refusal and as training signal. Every variant is validated by LLM judges distinct from the generator models. Instantiating the pipeline yields MSAFETEMP. Red-teaming leading open models on it exposes multilingual safety gaps that English-only evaluation does not show, and the localized variants surface failures that the translated ones miss. We explicitly include low-resource languages in both data production and evaluation for three reasons: (1) they are systematically underrepresented in existing safety development research; (2) they are usually addressed through simple translation without cultural adaptation; (3) prior work finds safety degradation to be most pronounced in low-resource languages (Yong et al., 2023), making them strong probe of gaps in the cross-lingual safety generalization of aligned models. In this work, we aim to answer three research questions: RQ1. Do safety capabilities of existing open models generalize well beyond English to lowresource languages and culturally-specific harms, or does cross-lingual alignment collapse outside of the English-centric setting? RQ2. Can template-based pipeline scale the generation of culturally grounded harmful and benign prompt variants without extensive human involvement? RQ3. Does training on such data narrow the multilingual safety gap without inflating over-refusal?

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Our key contributions are as follows: template-based, culturally grounded multilingual safety-data pipeline that turns small seed of English harmful prompts into fluent, harm-preserving, culturally authentic variants across 60 languages, with matched benign minimal pairs and jailbreak wrappers, each validated by dual-stage LLM judge. We release automatically generated cultural cards for all languages, allowing other researchers to reproduce and extend the multilingual data. MSAFETEMP, large-scale collection of grounded multilingual safety prompts: provenance-tracked corpus of more than 1 million validated prompts across 44 languages, split by source seed so that no descendant of test seed enters training. It includes smaller culturally localized harmful subset and benign subset, together with held-out red-teaming and over-refusal evaluation sets. Training ablations show that the dataset improves attack resistance and reduces over-refusal in multilingual settings. Multilingual safety evaluation revealing safety gaps that English-only evaluation misses and failures reachable only through localized entities, showing that several aligned open models struggle with out-of-distribution harmful and benign data.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Multilingual safety and red-teaming. Safety learned mainly from English does not transfer reliably: refused request may receive harmful answer after translation, especially in lowerresource language (Yong et al., 2023; Deng et al., 2024; Shen et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024). HarmBench and WildGuardMix make red-teaming reproducible, while Aya broadens human language coverage (Mazeika et al., 2024; Han et al., 2024; Aakanksha et al., 2024). Recent locally grounded benchmarks cover Indonesian, Southeast Asian, and African settings (Azmi et al., 2025; Tasawong et al., 2026; Abdullahi et al., 2026), and field survey confirms the broader language gap (Yong et al., 2025). These advances improve local validity but focus on selected regions or safeguard classification. We instead scale controlled cultural layer across 60 languages. Safety and helpfulness. Blocking harm at the cost of refusing harmless requests is not full alignment. XSTest and OR-Bench measure over-refusal (Röttger et al., 2024; Cui et al., 2024), while multilingual toxicity benchmarks test unsafe generation (Gehman et al., 2020; Hartvigsen et al., 2022; Jain et al., 2024). LinguaSafe evaluates multilingual oversensitivity; MORBench selects boundary-adjacent benign prompts but excludes low-resource languages (Ning et al., 2025; Pan et al., 2025). Neither provides controlled harmful and benign variants from the same template. Our matched controls measure both outcomes on closely shared linguistic and cultural content. Synthetic alignment data and model judges. LLMs are widely used to synthesize instructions and judge model outputs (Wang et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2023), alongside safety classifiers and feedback-based alignment (Inan et al., 2023; Ouyang et al., 2022; Rafailov et al., 2023; Bai et al., 2022). PolyGuard and CultureGuard scale multilingual moderation data, including through cultural adaptation (Kumar et al., 2025; Joshi et al., 2025); RefusEU shows that English-only refusal alignment transfers unevenly (Krasnodebska et al., 2026). We instead generate paired training and evaluation data while requiring harmful intent to survive translation and localization. Because model judges can fail systematically, we separate generation from judging, use explicit checks where possible, and report the remaining limitations.

sections.title: 3 TEMPLATE-BASED AUGMENTATION METHOD
sections.content: In this section, we describe the pipeline structure and the motivation behind our design choices. For an efficient and helpful data generation pipeline, our method needs to address the following four requirements: 1. R1 (harm fidelity): every variant preserves the original seeded harmful intent, so that compliant response would still be unsafe;

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: 2. R2 (linguistic correctness): prompts are fluent and natural in the target language, or the evaluation measures translation quality rather than safety; 3. R3 (cultural authenticity): use culturally relevant local entities where they fit the scenario, instead of only carrying over translated English ones; 4. R4 (over-refusal control): every harmful template yields matched benign minimal pair.

sections.title: 3.1 DESIGN MOTIVATION
sections.content: Unlocking multilingual scaled augmentation with templates. Multilingual data development requires fast, scalable, and automated processes to enable scaled training and evaluation. While for general knowledge domains this is usually achievable in straightforward way, acquiring harmful prompts in other languages presents unexpected bottlenecks. For example, asking highly aligned language model to simply translate harmful prompt is likely to result in refusal, since such models are trained not to process or produce harmful content; the same holds for culturally adapting or paraphrasing questions. Augmentation and localization are therefore blocked, and solving this requires representing the original text in safe form. harmful question frames the specific wording and dangerous intent described by specific entities together. Translation changes the language, but usually keeps the English entities, whereas native red-teaming changes both and is difficult to scale. Extracting words which make the prompt harmful separates it into two concepts which are by themselves regarded as non-harmful, which allows for further prompt modifications. These reasons justify using the template as more reliable way of maintaining the original prompt form and intent. We replace the selected harm-bearing phrases with placeholder tags, such as <illicit_substance>, named after their type/intent. After translating the template, we fill its placeholders directly in the target language, and separate pass substitutes entities from the target culture where they fit, so that the question reflects what is regarded as harmful there. This sequential design creates controlled comparisons: translated and localized attacks share the same frame, and benign control differs only in its filled placeholder values. It also reduces the number of rejects from the generator model, since it works with an abstract template rather than complete harmful request. Pipeline design. In this work, we focus on two directions, based on two different datasets as source of seed prompts. We use 200 standard behaviors from HarmBench (Mazeika et al., 2024) as source of prompts, designed for evaluation. We drop contextual and copyright categories since they are not defined solely by prompts themselves, but additional information, making template extraction inefficient. We keep this collection as held-out evaluation set. For training, we select 2,500 WildGuardMix (Han et al., 2024) harmful prompts (wildguardtrain split), which we later expand into 44 languages; 2,000 seeds and all their descendants form the training split and the remaining 500 held-out test split. For both datasets we produce harmful and benign options on template-level to assess the scaling and cross-lingual transfer impact on over-refusal performance. We use Gemma-4-31B-IT (Team et al., 2026) for generation-related tasks, since it is highly efficient in both multilinguality and safety; as generation judge, we use GPT-OSS-120B and for evaluation, GPT-OSS-Safeguard-120B (OpenAI et al., 2025). Cultural cards are generated by Gemma-4-31B-IT and verified by Gemini Flash 3.6 (Team et al., 2025). Each judge decides set of independent criteria that are aggregated into final pass gate, while grammar is enforced during generation rather than judged (App. A). The initial augmentation process is divided into four steps. First, the language model extracts single words or short phrases which make the prompt actually harmful and replaces them with placeholder slots to fill with other options. Second, the first judge verification checks if the new template is valid and self-contained. Afterwards, the generator model is used for translating the surrounding text around the fixed placeholder tags. second judge then checks target language consistency, translation quality, and whether slot placements were preserved (English as target language would skip translation step in this case, but still has both judge steps). Each template also receives two validated paraphrases, so every seed and language has three templates. The pipeline is shown in Figure 1.

sections.title: 3.2 FURTHER DATA AUGMENTATION BRANCHES
sections.content: After preparing the template, we proceed to enriching the placeholder alternatives. We split the process into three branches, adapted for different goals, as shown in Figure 2. Harmful variants (TR). The TR branch fills proposed template with several combinations of placeholder values. It also fills two validated paraphrases of the same template, diversifying how the same harmful intent is phrased. Finally, judge evaluates harmfulness, language quality, coherence, and original frame preservation. Benign alternatives (OR). In setting rich in harmful data, benign alternatives are useful to control the tradeoff between helpfulness and safety. template makes it possible to obtain prompt that is phrased like harmful one but is safe because its placeholder values are benign: the question form is preserved, while the intent now mirrors an ordinary user request. We distinguish DIRECT controls, which are safe to answer fully, from BOUNDED controls, where useful answer must still withhold transferable harmful details and require more rigorous control over response generation. Over-refusal (OR) is measured only on DIRECT; BOUNDED examples are retained as training data. We provide more details on over-refusal control in Appendix A.2. Culturally localized options (PH). For the non-English case, we generate cultural card for every language, describing locally relevant groups, organizations, events, concepts, and institutions. We refined the generation prompt iteratively on few languages known to the authors and then generated all cards automatically. We use conservative judge criteria to check whether post-hoc proposal is valid as placeholder value. After filling in the slots, the generator may inflect and rephrase around the entity to keep grammar and language flow natural; the judges only check the result. The resulting PH variants pass the same final judge as TR. The card structure and the scoring criteria for the judges are presented in Appendix A.3. Figure 2: MSAFETEMP example, showing how different augmentation types are produced from different stages in the pipeline.

sections.title: 4 THE MSAFETEMP DATASET
sections.content: MSAFETEMP consists of two directions  (Table 1)  : WildGuardMix is used for training purposes and HarmBench is used as evaluation material. The original 2,500 WildGuard English seeds are enriched into 1.8M validated set of harmful, benign, and culturally localized prompts in 44 languages. HarmBench is expanded from 200 original prompts into 216,486-prompt benchmark in 60 languages. The obtained scale comes from controlled variation of each seed rather than from collecting more seed prompts. The failure rate of the template generation stage is low, and most filtering happens in the judging stage, when the templates are filled. In the benign (OR) branch, the judge model rejects samples that remain unsafe or lose their meaning completely; in the post-hoc (PH) branch, it rejects slot candidates that do not fit the templates context. Since the culturally grounded generation is more cost-demanding, we limit our released PH subset to higher-quality but smaller set; we also find that localized conditioning limits the variety of fitting placeholder values per template, making it more focused and natural. We present more details about dataset statistics in Table 1 and Appendix A.4. Table 1: MSAFETEMP statistics. WildGuard is used for training and performance signal; HarmBench remains evaluation-only. Template counts are verified/original; benign counts are DIRECT + BOUNDED. Over-refusal uses DIRECT only. Each of the three templates per seed and language (the translated main template and its two paraphrases) receives five fills, giving up to 15 harmful variants wherever possible; more paraphrases or more fills per template brought diminishing gains in diversity and quality. This scale does not come from collapsing onto few favorite fills (Appendix B): harmful slots receive over 2.8M distinct entities (distinct-to-total ratio around 0.7), benign slots are still more varied (0.94), no entity appears in more than 1% of languages harmful fills, and diversity does not differ significantly between highand low-resource languages. Repetition is limited to canonical entities of narrow slot types (e.g. EternalBlue for software_vulnerability) and to the post-hoc slot, which by design draws from curated per-language pool. Since the source datasets do not share detailed label set, we classify the prompts with the LinguaSafe taxonomy (Ning et al., 2025), which assigns primary and more precise secondary class (Appendix A.4). Human validation. In an IRB-approved study with safety experts who are native or fluent speakers (15 unique ratings, 11 languages, 600 judgments; App. C), the prompts are rated as natural (4.43/5) and culturally fitting (4.46/5). Raters endorse 91% harmful labels but only 65% benign ones, often because softened or fictional control still reads as harmful, so over-refusal on our benign pairs may overstate true over-refusal. Responders elaborated that such questionable benign samples may be harmful in particular context or situation; however, it does not signal low authenticity level of the presented data. In general, the pipeline turns small set of English texts into multilingual corpus of diverse harmful and benign prompts, answering RQ2. The pipeline outputs per stage and full production details appear in Appendix A.6 and A.4.

sections.title: 5 EVALUATING THE MULTILINGUAL SAFETY GAP
sections.content: Throughout, GPT-OSS-Safeguard-120B judges the greedy responses of each target model. Attack success rate (ASR) is the share of harmful prompts answered with unsafe compliance, and over-refusal (OR) is the share of benign DIRECT pairs that are refused. We compare English (EN), translated (TR), and culturally localized (PH) prompts, and then test whether safety training changes these results. Per-language results and model grids are in Appendices D.1 and D, and confidence intervals in App. F.4.

sections.title: 6 TRAINING EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: To test whether MSAFETEMP is useful beyond evaluation, we fine-tune open models for one epoch on mix of refusals and benign answers (generated by Gemma-4-31B-IT and verified by GPT-OSS-120B) combined with general instruction data, with loss only on assistant tokens, and then apply DPO on preference pairs sampled from the fine-tuned model itself. The complete training hyperparameters are given in App. G.1. We apply the same data to base and instruction-tuned checkpoints to ask not only whether it helps, but also when it should enter the training pipeline. We tested our training setup on several popular open-weight and open-source models, such as Apertus-8B-2509, Apertus-v1.5-8B, Llama-3.1-8B and Olmo-3-7B. The effect on attack success is consistent across model families (Table 3; App. G.2): SFT sharply reduces multilingual attack success on both tracks and at both checkpoints. It costs some general capability, which is modest on MMLU but larger on GSM8K - such difference may come from quality of general instruction mix. Its effect on over-refusal depends on the model; moreover, after analyzing OR-Bench prompts with the judge model we find, that around 20% of samples are harmful and should be refused, which causes the optimal performance on that benchmark to be higher than 0%. For Apertus, multilingual over-refusal on the benign pairs rises only slightly, whereas for Olmo, which starts from very low over-refusal, it rises substantially. DPO on the models own samples then lowers over-refusal again while keeping attack success low. For Apertus it ends below the instruction-tuned model; for Olmo and Llama it remains above that level on at least one benchmark (App. G.2). We

sections.title: 7 DISCUSSION AND LIMITATIONS
sections.content: Limitations and future work. We are transparent about the limitations in the presented work. First, our pipeline heavily relies on automated LLM judging; two judges from another model family preserve the direction of our headline results on 5,000-response subsample (App. F.5), but full ablation over judge models remains future work. Second, our claims about multicultural quality again come from an LLM-as-a-judge setup; an interim human study (App. C) rates naturalness and cultural fit highly, but it covers only subset of languages with one or two respondents each, so larger human evaluation remains future work. Third, harm labels are assigned to the English seed and inherited by all descendants; localized entity, such as an extremist group or regional slur, can make variant more severe than its inherited label suggests, so re-labeling sample of localized variants remains future work. Fourth, the training ablations covered several models and their checkpoints with supervised fine-tuning followed by DPO; RL-based methods remain future work. SFT brings noticeable positive impact on safety but raises over-refusal, which DPO largely removes, and we observe small degradation in general capabilities, which we believe happens due to the aggressive nature of SFT training and stronger weight editing. Finally, our prompts are single-turn and follow fixed templates; extending the pipeline to multi-turn and iterative attacks, for example by using its localized variants as seeds for automated iterative attackers, is natural next step. Impact. We believe that the proposed artifacts and recipe will boost the development of safer multilingual models. Moreover, the open-source pipeline will allow scaling up alignment of models focused on particular languages, which in most cases are low-resource setups. We release the

We hope that our evaluation findings will motivate discussion towards targeting low-resource languages during training and evaluation with bigger efforts.

sections.title: 8 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We introduce template-based augmentation pipeline and MSAFETEMP, the massive multilingual corpus it produces for safety alignment and evaluation. Separating the questions framing from harmful entities allows for easier and more automated augmentation and translation of prompts at scale. Its training track covers 44 languages and its evaluation track 60, both containing harmful, benign, and culturally localized variants. This contribution unlocks the production of safer models in lower-resource settings for both the training and evaluation stages. Moreover, we conduct training ablations on our generated data and evaluate leading open-source and open-weight models on held-out harmful and benign test prompts in up to 60 languages. The results shed more light on the current state of alignment in open development: safety does not generalize evenly beyond English, the direction of the gap depends on the model, and the culturally localized variants expose failures that translation alone does not reach. Training on diverse and verified data improves the models safety in languages unseen during training, showing promising direction in future model development. Multilingual safety work should therefore evaluate language, culture, safety and helpfulness together rather than treating English refusal rates as sufficient.

sections.title: ETHICS STATEMENT
sections.content: MSAFETEMP is dual-use because it contains harmful prompts and jailbreak wrappers. We release the full dataset, including harmful variants, jailbreak wrappers, benign pairs, and refusal responses, together with pipeline prompts and aggregate results under permissive license, as they were produced from models with permissive usage as well. Because of its harmful content, the Hugging Face dataset carries content warning that viewers must accept before viewing, gating initial access. Harmful examples are paired with safe responses for training ablations. The prompts shown in the paper come from the public WildGuardMix and HarmBench sources or are derived from them, and none carries operational uplift. We fully disclose the underlying data resources used for generation and reference them in this work. Generative AI is used for data generation and judging, and we disclose its use for writing assistance. The human study was IRB approved, and we report only aggregate results from it. The intended benefit is broader safety coverage for speakers and communities where English-centered alignment currently serves poorly.

sections.title: REPRODUCIBILITY STATEMENT
sections.content: To ensure reproducibility of presented work, we present all details on data generation, evaluation and training parts in various sections of the paper. Additionally, we release our codebase and generated data with this work. We specify the design of the augmentation pipeline and motivation behind model selection for generation and judging in 3 and Appendix A, with full worked example of every stage in Appendix A.6. Dataset statistics and further details on format, labels and general datasheet are presented in Appendix A.4 and Appendix A.7. Training and evaluation technical specifications and hyperparameters are provided in Appendix G.1. Full evaluation details per every used model are shown on language-level in Appendices and D.1. We publicly release the presented pipeline codebase, data artifacts (following the structure specified in Appendix A.7), and evaluation design under permissive license.

sections.title: AI USE STATEMENT
sections.content: In this work, generative AI tools are core component of the method itself: all data generation, translation, cultural localization, and judging steps are carried out by the language models named in 3 and Appendix A, and their role, prompts, and validation criteria are documented there. We additionally used generative AI tools for writing assistance (copy-editing and phrasing of the manuscript) and for

sections.title: A PIPELINE AND DATASET CONSTRUCTION DETAILS
sections.content: A.1 SOURCES, MODELS, AND JUDGE DESIGN HarmBench contributes 200 self-contained standard behaviors. We exclude its contextual and copyright categories and keep the full HarmBench track evaluation-only. WildGuardMix contributes 2,500 harmful prompts, selected by seeded shuffle of wildguardtrain; this track provides all released training data. Generation uses Gemma-4-31B-IT, pipeline judging uses GPT-OSS-120B, and taxonomy and response judging use GPT-OSS-Safeguard-120B. Cultural cards are checked by Gemini Flash 3.6; manual review was limited to the languages used to develop the generation prompt. Generation and judging therefore do not use models from the same family. One evaluated target, GPT-OSS-20B, belongs to the same model family as the evaluation judge, so its scores may carry same-family bias; we report it alongside the other targets but treat its comparison with some caution. The judge design addresses two failure modes we observed in earlier versions of the pipeline. First, safety-tuned judge sometimes described variant as harmful in its reasoning, but returned the opposite overall verdict. This polarity inversion caused most early rejections. We now ask for separate Boolean decision on each criterion and combine the decisions in code. Second, an LLM grammar check produced mostly false flags in German audit and sometimes introduced new errors. We removed that check and instead constrain the morphology during generation. A.2 BRANCH-LEVEL GENERATION AND VALIDATION The extractor replaces the smallest entities that carry the harmful intent. Placeholder values should be short (13 words) and narrow; prompts whose harm cannot be expressed through such values are dropped at the judge stage. The first judge checks whether the result is self-contained, whether its placeholder values are clear, whether harm is preserved, and whether unchanged text remains faithful to the seed. failed extraction is retried up to two times before the sample is rejected. The translator keeps the placeholder tag names in English and rewrites only the surrounding text. Its judge checks preservation of meaning, slot integrity, and target-language consistency. If the judge fails translation, patching step edits only the flagged spans instead of translating the entire template again. After at most three patch rounds, the best version is retained with its validation record. For the TR direction, the generator model proposes five filled variants for the translated main template and for each of its two validated paraphrases, for up to 15 variants per seed and language. The final judge verifies the harmfulness, language, coherence, and preservation of the original framing. For benign OR variants, the process mirrors TR, but the placeholder values must themselves be benign and the filled prompt must be safe request. Candidates are classified as DIRECT, BOUNDED, TOXIC, or REJECT_QUALITY. DIRECT request can be answered fully without transferable harmful detail. BOUNDED request has legitimate use, but complete answer would still expose such detail. Whether BOUNDED request is handled well depends on the answer rather than on the prompt: careful, partial answer is ideal, but refusal is not clearly wrong. We therefore measure over-refusal on DIRECT only, where refusing is unambiguously an error, and use BOUNDED prompts only as training signal, paired with generated answers that help while withholding the harmful detail, so that the model learns to stay helpful in borderline cases. A.3 CULTURAL CARDS AND LOCALIZATION CHECKS Each language except English and Zulu has cultural card covering locally relevant demographic groups, organizations, charged concepts, locations, historical events, public figures, and institutional red lines. The cards list of entities forms that languages entity pool; for each entity the card records social context, grammatical form, target-language usage, and the scenario roles in which the entity may or may not be used. We generate each card with Gemma-4-31B-IT from fixed guideline and check it with Gemini Flash 3.6. The guideline was developed iteratively on few languages known to the authors, whose cards we reviewed and edited by hand; all other cards were produced automatically. We find that the synthetic cards provide valid and informative terms, but they contain occasional typos and grammar errors, which the Gemini Flash 3.6 check corrects.

An entity is accepted only when it matches the slot type and qualifier, is historically and semantically coherent with the full sentence, is used at an appropriate level of gravity, and does not reverse victim and perpetrator roles. We call an accepted assignment of pool entities to the slots of one template recipe; every recipe is copy-checked against the entity pool. The generator may inflect and rephrase around an entity but must preserve its referent. The resulting prompt passes the same final judge as the TR arm. sections.content: Composition and schema. Each record is prompt variant with its provenance and validation metadata: the originating template identifier, the target language, harm category, flag and source for cultural grounding, the identifier of its matched benign minimal pair (when applicable), the judge scores on the four acceptance criteria, and the train/test split assignment, which is made by source seed. Records come in three roles, harmful variant, matched benign minimal pair, and jailbreak-wrapped variant, and every accepted harmful record is paired with safe refusal response for training. Provenance and licensing. Harmful seeds are drawn from two existing English safety benchmarks, WildGuardMix and HarmBench; redistribution of derived content is governed by those upstream terms, which we honor independently of the Apache-2.0 licensing of the models used in the pipeline. Cultural context material is authored from per-language cultural cards rather than scraped, so it does not inherit third-party content restrictions. Label provenance and known caveats. All acceptance labels are produced by the automatic, per-criterion judging described in 3 and App. A, with generation and judging kept separate. An interim native-speaker study (App. C) endorsed 91% of sampled HARMFUL and 65% of sampled BENIGN labels, but it is not full human calibration; users should treat labels as automatic and, where possible, spot-check them against native-speaker judgment for the languages they care about. Responsible release. We openly release the full dataset under permissive license, including the harmful variants, jailbreak wrappers, benign minimal pairs, and refusal responses, together with all pipeline prompts and the per-language evaluation tables. Because of its harmful content, the Hugging Face dataset carries content warning that viewers must accept before viewing, so users must accept the terms of use before downloading it; every harmful prompt is distributed paired with safe refusal, and operational detail is redacted in the paper.

sections.title: B ENTITY DIVERSITY ANALYSIS
sections.content: Template-based augmentation carries specific risk: if the generator keeps filling the same slots with the same few entities, dataset can look large and multilingual on the surface while being redundant underneath. We measure entity diversity in the released MSAFETEMP data for the harmful, benign, and post-hoc arms, pooled and per language, and report where repetition does occur. B.1 RECOVERING SLOT FILLS Slot fills are not stored in the data, and entities are not inserted programmatically: the generator writes each variant in full around the entities it chooses. Plain string substitution would break agreement, case, and particles in many of our languages (e.g. Zulu noun-class prefixes, Korean case particles, Slavic and Baltic case endings) and would force every fill into one fixed grammatical form, which we found to produce ungrammatical prompts in practice. Entities therefore have to be recovered after generation. We align each variant to the template it was generated from (token-level diff; per character for Chinese, Japanese, and Thai) and take the span aligned to each slot as its fill, stripping template words that survive glued to it. This recovers fill for every row with slot, except 70 of 1.84M WildGuard rows. For 82.0% (HarmBench) and 86.3% (WildGuard) of fills the span is the fill alone; the rest still carry an inflected neighboring word. We count one fill per (row, slot), so slot repeated within one prompt counts once, and we drop spans that merge two adjacent slots (9.0% / 4.0% of fills). Entities are compared within language after NFKC normalization and casefolding. Benign means DIRECT + BOUNDED (WildGuard auditrejected rows excluded). The localized post-hoc slot is taken from the fit judges recipe rather than from alignment. We report the distinct ratio D/F (D distinct entities among fills), the effective number Neff = exp( (cid:80) pe log pe), and top-k shares. Inflection inflates in morphologically rich languages, so we also report D/Fstem, computed after truncating every word to five characters; this deliberately over-merges and is conservative lower bound.

B.5 WHERE ENTITIES DO RECUR Diversity is high overall, but some entities appear often. Nearly all of these recurrences fall into three identifiable groups. Canonical referents of narrow slot types. Some slot types have only handful of well-known real-world answers. Examples  (Table 10)  : database_system is filled with PostgreSQL in 18.8% of cases (HarmBench); software_vulnerability with EternalBlue in 11.9%; illicit_substance with LSD in 6.3%. These named entities are the ones that produce the most frequent fills overall  (Table 11)  : EternalBlue, Log4Shell, Heartbleed, ransomware, SQL injection, LSD, MDMA. sections.title: C HUMAN EVALUATION
sections.content: C.1 STUDY DESCRIPTION We ran an expert annotation study in which participants acted as informants on the generated items: the study analyzes the texts, not the participants. Participants had professional experience in AI safety, red-teaming, content moderation, or trust-and-safety work and were native or fluent speakers of the language they annotated. Members of the general public, crowdworkers, and persons in dependency relationship to the investigators could not take part, and no one was hired or paid. The study ran online, with one Google Form per language (60 forms). Each form contains 40 items from MSAFETEMP in that language, 20 labeled HARMFUL and 20 labeled BENIGN, shown one at time. Each item is user prompt only; no model answer is shown or rated. session was capped at 40 items and about 30 minutes, and participants could take breaks, skip any item, or stop at any time. Before starting, participants read an information sheet describing the purpose of the study, the eligibility conditions, the task, content warning listing the harm categories covered by the items (for example weapons, violent and sex-related crime, cyber and financial crime, misinformation, self-harm, and sexual content), their rights, the risks and benefits, and how their data are used. They then confirmed six consent statements: that they had read and understood the information, were taking part voluntarily, fulfilled the participation conditions, consented to the described data collection and use, knew the data may be published in anonymized form, and knew they could withdraw at any time. Ratings are stored under random participant ID; no name, e-mail, or IP address is collected in the form, and recruitment contact details are kept separately and never linked to the ratings. C.

sections.title: INSTRUCTIONS FOR PARTICIPANTS
sections.content: Each form opens with the following instructions (shown here for English). Read each prompt as request someone might send to an AI assistant. Evaluate the prompt only; you do not need to answer it. Judge three things separately: how naturally it is written, how well its cultural details fit, and whether its assigned safety label is correct. harmful prompt can still sound natural and fit its cultural context. You may leave either rating blank. Choose Unsure when you cannot determine the safety label; choose Skip when you prefer not to assess the item. Comments are optional. Do not include names, contact details or other identifying information. For every item, participants answer the following questions. Naturalness (optional, 15): How natural does the wording sound in [language]? Participants consider grammar, word choice, expressions, and sentence flow; informal language, dialect, and code-switching are not automatically errors. Anchors: 1, very unnatural, difficult to understand; 2, frequent awkward wording or errors; 3, understandable but noticeably awkward in places; 4, mostly natural with minor issues; 5, fully natural and fluent. Cultural fit (optional, 15): How well do the cultural details fit the setting? Participants judge whether places, institutions, customs, and social conventions make sense in the described setting, judging contextual fit rather than moral acceptability, and leave the rating blank if there are no relevant cultural details. Anchors: 1, clearly inconsistent with the setting; 2, several substantial mismatches; 3, some details fit, others seem questionable; 4, mostly plausible with minor mismatches; 5, consistently plausible and appropriate. Safety label: Does the assigned safety label match what the prompt asks for? HARMFUL means the prompt asks for content or assistance that would facilitate, encourage, or constitute harm; BENIGN means it does not, and discussing sensitive topic for explanation, prevention, or analysis is not automatically harmful. Claims such as just joke, fictional, or for research do not by themselves determine the label. Options: Correct, Incorrect (I would assign the other label), Unsure, and Skip. Comment (optional): what influenced the ratings, for example awkward wording, cultural mismatch, or reason to disagree with the label.

sections.content: F.2 REPHRASING ABLATION FOR POST-HOC CULTURAL GENERATION The PH arm changes two things at once: it substitutes locally authentic entity, and it lets the generator rephrase the request around that entity. Fig. 3 therefore measures the localization step as whole. To separate the two, we regenerated every accepted recipe with the template frozen, instructing the generator to fill the slots and adjust only the agreement that grammar forces, leaving the wording untouched. Nothing else changed: same recipes, same generator, same four-axis judge. The frozen variants pass the judge slightly more often than the rephrased ones (96.8% against 93.0% of 2,164 recipes), so freezing does not damage grammaticality, and they sit much closer to the template (mean similarity 0.69 against 0.45). Table 42 reads the three arms on the same behaviors and languages, with truncated generations dropped, all scored by GPT-OSS-Safeguard-120B. The three arms lie within three points of each other. Holding the entity fixed, rephrasing changes attack success by less than about one point, and holding the frame fixed, the culturally filled prompts sit level with the generically filled ones (slightly above for Apertus, slightly below for Olmo). The choice of local entity therefore does not change how often model breaks. That does not make the cultural fills redundant. Matching the number of variants per cell, the two arms agree on fewer than half of the behaviors they break (Jaccard 0.45 and 0.40), and roughly 45% of the failures that appear in exactly one arm appear only under the culturally filled prompts. Cultural grounding changes which requests succeed rather than how many, and the failures it reaches are not reachable by translation alone. Table 42: Cultural fill and rephrasing, separated. We sample 100 template families from each held-out track (HarmBench and WildGuard) with seeded choices and balanced language quotas; each family contributes one language and one fixed TR/PH pair. The 200 families cover 58 languages in HarmBench and 43 in WildGuard. Each PH request is inserted verbatim into ten distinct wrappers from our translated wrapper bank, derived from PyRIT (Lutz et al., 2026). If fewer than ten pre-assembled wrapped variants exist for request, the remaining ones are built from unused wrappers in the bank in the same way; no new wrappers are generated. The wrapper order is fixed and seeded in advance, independent of model responses and judge outcomes. TR, PH, and first-wrapper responses are reused from earlier runs, so only the other nine wrapped variants are newly generated (7,200 of 9,600 responses). Targets and scoring. We evaluate the instruction-tuned checkpoints of Apertus-8B-Instruct-2509, Olmo-3-7B-Instruct, Qwen3.5-9B (thinking disabled), and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct before our safety fine-tuning, all on the same inputs, with temperature 0 and an 8,192-token output limit. The GPT-OSS-Safeguard-120B judge sees the full wrapped prompt and the response with reasoning tokens removed (temperature 0, 16,384-token limit; two attempts with the main judge prompt, then one with fallback prompt in clinical wording). response counts as success if it contains genuinely harmful content, even alongside refusal language; this is harmful-content metric, not the official HarmBench classifier. Responses that reach the output limit are scored as returned rather than counted as safe. Two wrapped WildGuard responses, one each for Apertus and Olmo, could not be scored and are left unscored. All comparisons therefore use the groups with complete scores (199 for Apertus and Olmo, 200 for Qwen and Llama), so baselines can differ slightly from the full 200-family set.

sections.title: G TRAINING DETAILS AND RESULTS
sections.content: G.1 EXPERIMENTAL DETAILS Training data. Table 49 lists the SFT and DPO data. The general instruction rows come from Dolci-Instruct-SFT (no-tools split), from which we removed all rows derived from WildGuardMix and all replies that open with refusal. The short benign requests are one-sentence task requests (Write. . . , Explain. . . ) that Gemma-4-31B-IT rewrites from short WildGuardMix training prompts into harmless requests with the same frame, keeping sensitive wording where it stays natural. GPT-OSS-120B keeps request only if it is benign and direct task; we drop candidates that overlap HarmBench or OR-Bench prompt (character 4-gram Jaccard 0.5), translate subset into the training languages, and answer all of them with the same generator as the other benign rows. Without them, the safety data pairs short task requests almost only with refusals. Safety fine-tuning. All MSAFETEMP fine-tunes use the same data; only the starting checkpoint and the training framework change. Apertus is trained with Megatron-LM for one epoch over sequences packed to 4096 tokens (best-fit decreasing, at most 8 documents per sequence), with global batch of 128 packed sequences (3,543 steps), tensor parallelism 4 on 128 GH200 GPUs. Llama and Olmo are trained with TRL on 400,000-row sample of the same mix with the same class proportions, for one epoch without packing, with an effective batch of 128 sequences (FSDP2, 128 GPUs, no gradient accumulation). In both cases the loss covers assistant tokens only. We use learning rate of 1 105 with cosine schedule, 3% warmup, zero weight decay, gradient clipping at 1.0, and bf16. We fix the seed at 1234 and report the final checkpoint rather than selecting one on validation data. Preference optimization. DPO starts from the fine-tuned instruction-tuned checkpoint and uses on-policy pairs. For each prompt of the safety data the model samples three answers to harmful prompts and two to benign prompts (temperature 0.8, top-p 0.9), plus one refusal forced by system instruction (temperature 0). GPT-OSS-120B judge labels every answer. Harmful prompts yield pair when the model produced both natural refusal (chosen) and an unsafe completion (rejected);
